title: Savitri, born of a prayer
hookLine: a king offers the Savitri mantra for years, and the goddess of that prayer gives him a daughter who sees clearly
carry: the gayatri: a prayer for light in the mind

cards: Has there ever been a woman as devoted as Draupadi? Still in the forest, Yudhishthira puts the question to the sage Markandeya. He has watched her suffer beside him through all of it: the hall, the exile, the forest.

Markandeya answers the way Brihadashva did, with a story. There was a princess, he says, named Savitri. And her story, like Nala's, starts long before the trouble does, with a father who wanted a child.

teach.b: Ashvapati, king of the Madras, is good, generous and childless. So he takes up a discipline: he eats sparingly, keeps his senses in check, and makes offerings in the fire with the Savitri mantra, for years.
At last the goddess of that mantra rises out of the sacred fire and grants him a daughter. He names the girl Savitri, after the goddess who gave her. Now, the teaching hidden in her name.

teach.h: THE SAVITRI MANTRA IS THE GAYATRI.
teach.b: The Savitri mantra is the verse most Hindus know as the Gayatri mantra, chanted after the words om bhur bhuvah svah.
It comes from the Rig Veda, and it's addressed to Savitr, the sun as the one who stirs all things to life; that's why it's also called the Savitri.
Its heart is one request: may that light inspire our minds. It doesn't ask for wealth, or even for a child. It asks to see clearly.

It's taught at the sacred thread ceremony and chanted in many homes at sunrise. So, as many readers notice, the princess of this story is a daughter of the prayer for light. And watch how clearly she sees.
She grows so radiant that no man dares to ask for her hand.
So her father does something unusual: go yourself, he tells her, and find a husband worthy of you. She travels through forests and hermitages, and comes home with a name.
A king called Dyumatsena went blind, lost his kingdom, and lives in a forest hermitage. His son is Satyavan. He's the one I've chosen.
For today: when you have to choose, one of the oldest Hindu prayers doesn't say give me what I want.

teach.h: A DAUGHTER OF THE PRAYER FOR LIGHT.
teach.b: It says light up my mind.

how: The story of Savitri and Satyavan is told by the sage Markandeya to Yudhishthira in the Vana Parva; her father prays with the Savitri mantra, the Rig Veda verse to Savitr that most Hindus know as the Gayatri mantra.

games.q: a friend hears your family chanting the Gayatri mantra and asks if it's a wish for good grades. what does it actually ask for?
o: that the light of Savitr, the sun, inspire our minds.
games.why: it asks to see clearly. in the story, Savitri, born of that prayer, goes out and chooses with clear eyes.

practice: If you know the Gayatri mantra, say it once, slowly, facing whatever light is near you, a window, a lamp, the morning. If you don't know it, ask in your own words for a clear mind about one choice in front of you.
If you don't pray, simply sit facing the light, breathe, and let the choice be seen as it is.

wordCard.voice: Savitri. Named for the goddess of the prayer to the sun, the girl who goes out into the world and sees clearly enough to choose.
